extracted.intended_audience: readers and contributors of Nature (scientists, engineers, reviewers, and scientific authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and reviewing scientific or technical books (handbooks, treatises, field guides) for an academic journal's review column, focusing on clarity, accuracy, scope, audience-suitability, and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit verbatim quotations; summarise and cite
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid long verbatim quotations in a handbook; retain summaries and give references to the original paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example critique: in a book of 318 pages, 140 are verbatim quotations causing incoherence; suggested that the next edition 'retain only the summary and give the necessary reference to the original paper.' Long quotations reduce the author's synthesis and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and scientific/literary homogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: A handbook should provide a clear résumé of existing facts and theories welded together into a consistent whole possessing some sort of literary as well as scientific homogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handbooks are expected to synthesise material into a consistent narrative rather than read as a patchwork of other authors' texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handbook purpose: summarise established knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Books on scientific or technical subjects have a definite function distinct from journals; one does not look to them for new discoveries, but for a clear résumé of existing facts and theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the book meets the expected function for its genre (reference/synthesis vs original research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give original exposition where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Material written 'from the author's own pen' (original descriptions/explanations) is valuable and welcomed amid quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight and weigh original chapters (e.g., theory chapters) positively when they contribute insight beyond quoted sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title should accurately reflect scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The title must reflect the book's true focus (e.g., if it treats experimental work chiefly, it might be better titled 'Experimental Machine Design').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A misleading title sets wrong expectations; reviewers note when scope implied by title does not match content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness for declared remit
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general treatise, the book should cover expected core topics (e.g., correct proportioning of common machine parts); omission is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether omissions (faults of omission rather than commission) undermine the book's usefulness for its intended purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical accuracy of data and formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical values and formulae must be correct (e.g., correct modulus values and torsion-modulus expressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should check and point out slips (e.g., modulus of elasticity misquoted as 40,000,000 lb/in^2 vs expected values) and incorrect formulae (torsion modulus expressions), since such errors can mislead practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical originality and ingenuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical treatment that is new and ingenious is a positive attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the book has omissions, original analytical contributions are of great value to practitioners and should be praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical relevance of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental investigations should be of practical interest and teach lessons useful to designers (e.g., on bursting strength, gearing, fly-wheels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise experiments that have direct implications for preventing design failures and improving practice; recommend further research or incorporation into future editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and accuracy of illustrations and diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations should be clear without excessive detail and diagrams must be correct (not crude or incorrect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good illustrations aid comprehension; poor or incorrect figures (e.g., an unexpected stuffing-box drawing) detract from the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness of experimental methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Friction and other experiments must be carried out in a reliable manner; crude methods yield misleading results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique experimental methodology and flag results that may be unreliable due to crude methods or poor controls (example referenced p. 107).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and determinative value in species accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: In field guides and flora lists, include popular and scientific names, localities, and diagnostic features sufficient for identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether species descriptions provide determinative value; notes that 'features are of little determinative value' is a negative point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational continuity and adequate descriptive chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive chapters should provide continuity and enough background before specialised topics are introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism given where a book delays treatment of the main subject (e.g., not introducing wireless telegraphy until halfway through) or where descriptive material 'is slight and lacks continuity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of photographic/accurate illustrations for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs or well-rendered illustrations help travellers/readers obtain a fair idea of flora/fauna and assist in identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive note on 'good illustrations taken from the author's photographs'; poor illustrations (e.g., of myna) are a detriment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in historical/interpretative identifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing historical or biblical identifications (plants, animals), follow authoritative guides and avoid obvious mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: following Canon Tristram and Dr. Post for Biblical plant names; flag and correct obvious misidentifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate species selection for target region/audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of species should reflect the needs of the intended audience (e.g., travellers in India need the common/adjutant stork and characteristic Indian species in illustrations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omitting important local species or illustrating non-characteristic species is a lapse in judgement for a regional field guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of prose and grammatical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should be grammatical and well-written; poor grammar and awkward sentences are noted against the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers call for improved sentence construction in future editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit and critical account of experiments and views in surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly surveys should present explicit, critical accounts of experiments and views (giving due credit and tracing the evolution of ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a survey 'presents an explicit and critical account of the experiments and views elaborated by Metschnikoff, Ehrlich, and Pfeiffer'—this is commended as suitable for specialist audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match depth to intended readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the level of exposition matches the audience (e.g., botanical summaries suitable for plant pathologists; introductory accounts for beginners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A book 'likely to prove of interest to the expert as well as to the beginner' earns positive mention; mismatches (too elementary or too advanced) should be flagged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission and correspondence policy for letters/manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial policy: the Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by correspondents; cannot return or correspond with writers of rejected manuscripts; no notice taken of anonymous communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors should not expect returned manuscripts or personalised correspondence for rejected items and should avoid anonymous submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain expertise required for interdisciplinary methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners (e.g., statisticians) applying methods to specialised fields (e.g., astronomy) must be intimately acquainted with the technical domain as well as their statistical tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique arises when statisticians apply methods without domain understanding; advise collaboration or deep domain study before applying general methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate statistical measures for the data
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer statistical measures suited to the nature of the relationship (e.g., use correlation ratio rather than coefficient of correlation when the regression curve is not linear or the range of quantities is large).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correlation ratio 'expresses the degree of approximation to a smooth curve' and may be more appropriate in astronomical statistics than the simple correlation coefficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware selection bias and specialised samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Data sets specialised for particular properties (e.g., red or high-proper-motion stars) are not representative and can lead to misleading conclusions when generalised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should disclose selection criteria and reviewers should judge whether conclusions overreach given the data's provenance (example: Cape photographic revision focused on red/photographically faint stars).
